title: Troubleshoot and Solve Non-Conformance Problems and Recommend Corrective Action

lessons.title: Recognising and containing non-conformances
lessons.html:
What is a non-conformance?

A non-conformance is any product, process or practice that does not meet a requirement. Requirements come from the law (such as the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations), the abattoir's procedures, customer specifications and safety rules.

Examples

  • Product: carcasses with gut content, carcasses above dispatch temperature, wrong labels.
  • Process: steriliser below temperature, ineffective stunning, chiller overloaded.
  • Practice: workers not washing hands, guards removed, rough animal handling.
  • Records: missing temperature checks, unsigned cleaning sheets.

Sources of information

Non-conformances are found through your own monitoring, inspector findings, internal and external audits, laboratory results, customer complaints and worker reports. Encourage workers to report problems without fear; hidden problems are the most dangerous.

Step 1: Contain

When you find a non-conformance, first stop it from getting worse:

  • Stop the unsafe practice or process.
  • Identify and hold affected product, for example place carcasses on hold in the chiller and label them.
  • Inform the meat inspector if product safety is affected, and the foreman or manager.
  • If people are at risk, make the area safe first.

Step 2: Assess the impact

How many carcasses are affected? Since when? Has any product been dispatched? Is it a food safety, legal, welfare, safety or quality issue? The answers decide how urgent the response is and who must be told.

lessons.title: Finding the root cause
lessons.html:
Fix the cause, not just the symptom

Trimming a contaminated carcass fixes the symptom. Finding out why it was contaminated and stopping it fixes the problem.

Gather facts

  • Look at the place where it happened.
  • Talk to the workers involved, calmly and without blame.
  • Check records: steriliser logs, maintenance records, training records, temperature charts.
  • Note the time, the station, the people, the equipment and the animals involved.

Tool 1: The five whys

Ask why repeatedly until you reach a cause you can act on.

Carcasses arrive at dispatch above temperature. Why? They were not in the chiller long enough. Why? They were loaded early to meet a delivery time. Why? The kill started late. Why? The stunner failed at the start of the shift. Why? It was not tested and serviced as scheduled. Root causes: no stunner test before the shift and dispatch pressure overriding temperature rules.

Tool 2: Cause and effect (fishbone) thinking

Consider causes under headings:

HeadingQuestions
PeopleTrained? Enough staff? Tired? Supervised?
MethodIs there an SOP? Is it clear and followed?
MachinesWorking? Maintained? Correctly set?
MaterialsRight chemicals, bags, labels available?
AnimalsDirty, stressed, diseased, late?
EnvironmentHeat, condensation, lighting, space?
MeasurementThermometers calibrated? Checks done on time?

There is often more than one cause. Use data to confirm the cause, rather than guessing.

lessons.title: Recommending and verifying corrective action
lessons.html:
Choosing corrective action

Good corrective actions address the root cause and are practical. Compare options by:

  • Will it remove the cause and stop the problem returning?
  • Is it legal and safe?
  • How much will it cost and how long will it take?
  • Who must do it, and do they have the skills and authority?

Hierarchy of controls

Stronger actions change the system; weaker ones rely on people remembering. From strongest to weakest:

  1. Remove the cause (for example replace a faulty steriliser element).
  2. Engineer it out (an alarm on the chiller, an interlock on a guard).
  3. Change the procedure (add a stunner test to the start-up checklist).
  4. Train and supervise.
  5. Warn (a sign or reminder).

Often a combination works best.

Writing the recommendation

Write a short corrective action report:

  • Description of the non-conformance, date and place.
  • Immediate containment taken and product affected.
  • Root cause and the evidence for it.
  • Recommended corrective and preventive actions, with owner and deadline.
  • How effectiveness will be checked.

Verify

After the action, check that the problem has really stopped: review records, observe the station, check the trend over the following weeks. Close the report only when the evidence shows it worked. If not, look again at the root cause.

Key points

  • A non-conformance is anything that does not meet a legal, procedural, customer or safety requirement.
  • Contain first: stop the practice and hold affected product.
  • Use facts, the five whys and cause-and-effect headings to find root causes.
  • Prefer actions that change the system over reminders.
  • Verify that the action worked before closing the report.
